event: During the TIQUILA Task Order 1 STALKER FAT, the SGCS1 laptop Windows user accounts did not show a unique GCS ID (account showed only "APC"); no aircraft or flight involved.
component: SGCS1 laptop Windows user account names (hardware setup process)
failure_mode: The three program-specific accounts (Admin, APC, Payload Operator) were created without the unique kit number suffix that earlier single admin accounts carried.
contributing: Program request for three named accounts replaced the earlier SGCS1-XX naming convention

evidence.quote: During TO1 STALKER FAT, a test was conducted to identify is the GCS generated a unique ID. The Test failed and instead APC was observed.
For VXEP-35, it seems like the name of the accounts should be suffixed with -XX just as we have done in the past.
This is not connected to any release or the GCS Software, it is part of the GCS hardware setup process. It appears to be done.
For the TIQ program, I was explicitly asked to make 3 accounts: Admin, APC (Air Platform Controller, I think?), and Payload Operator.

team_view_in_comments: For VXEP-35, it seems like the name of the accounts should be suffixed with -XX just as we have done in the past.
reasoning: The FAT test expected a unique GCS ID and saw only the generic account name APC. The comments explain that the TIQ program accounts were set up without the kit number suffix used on earlier laptops, and that this is part of the GCS hardware setup process, not the GCS software. GCSS-82 was created and closed to append the kit number to each account.
notes: Squawk, not a flight incident. No Root Cause field; the explanation comes from Craig Burton and Michael Berger comments and GCSS-82.

event: While setting up SGCS1 during the TIQUILA TO1 STALKER FAT, the IMU display showed incorrect yaw and attitude; no flight involved, ticket canceled.
failure_mode: Incorrect yaw/attitude shown during ground setup; one note attributes it to an autopilot hardware failure, another to misreading the display.
contributing: Ticket also states the observation was human error (misreading information)

evidence.quote: During TO1 STALKER FAT - whilst setting up SGCS1, it was observed that the IMU showed the incorrect yaw/attitude.
Canceling issue as it was a result of human error (misreading information).
(Recommend removal - this behavior was a result of PTR-85 autopilot hardware failure.)

disagreement: The Root Cause field says "Incorrect interpretation of information." and the description says the observation was human error, but the Issue Status says "this behavior was a result of PTR-85 autopilot hardware failure." The second note names a real hardware fault, so the reading favored here is an autopilot fault, with low confidence because the ticket contradicts itself and PTR-85 is not in the export.

would_settle_it.what: Whether PTR-85 confirms an autopilot hardware failure on the same aircraft and that it explains the wrong IMU yaw/attitude during SGCS1 setup

reasoning: The ticket has two conflicting explanations: the description and Root Cause field call it misreading of information, while the Issue Status attributes the behavior to the PTR-85 autopilot hardware failure. There is no data, comment or attachment to choose between them. The more specific statement points to the autopilot, so the result is narrowed to avionics hardware with low confidence.
notes: No comments or attachments. PTR-85 is referenced in the text but not in the export (no folder under data/linked and not in the moved list). Tail not given.

event: Customer acceptance review for TIQUILA Task Order 1 found no plan or evidence for the mold and bacteria test required by the system requirement acceptance criteria; no aircraft event.
component: mold and bacteria test plan for system and transit case storage (acceptance criterion, SRD-59)
failure_mode: Required acceptance test for mold and bacteria had no defined requirement, test plan or evidence of compliance.
contributing: Earlier internal mold found in transit cases from missing silica packets and poor pocket airflow, fixed with the case manufacturer

evidence.quote: The system requirement acceptance criteria states to test Mould and Bacteria, within the time scales of Task Order 1.
Please include evidence for how Stalker intend to meet this requirement.
There was a mold issue due to the cases not having silica packets in each pocket and the pockets did not have adequate air flow + they were not dried before arriving to our facility
Storage and handling procedures that prevent mold growth (system is dried before being stored, thermal storage range specified) are outlined in the manual.

team_root_cause: No plan for testing of mold and bacteria
reasoning: This is a requirements compliance squawk, not a failure: the acceptance criteria call for a mold and bacteria test and the customer asked for evidence of how it would be met. The team field says there was no plan, and VA-406 shows the follow-up defined storage and handling procedures in the manual and traced an earlier mold problem to transit cases lacking silica packets and airflow. The finding matches the team root cause.
notes: Not a hardware or flight incident. System chosen as ground_equipment because the only physical mold finding was in transit cases; the core gap is a missing test plan. VA-413 (plan task) was canceled.

event: During HLB removal, a person suffered a minor cut/graze when their hand hit the edge of the fuselage top cutout; no flight involved.
component: fuselage top cutout edge at the lift battery (HLB) bay
failure_mode: Sharp, chipped cutout edge with little clearance; the hand whips into the edge when the stiff HLB power connector breaks loose during demating.
contributing: High force needed to demate the HLB power connector
Enlarged cutout specified in ENG-1344 was found not to have actually been implemented on fuselages
Edge material degraded by repeated battery exchanges

evidence.quote: an individual had a minor cut/graze caused during the removal of a HLB when coming in to contact with the edge of the fuselage.
We coordinated to enlarge the cutout for the fuselage to improve access and hopefully reduce the tendency for folks to run their hand into the edge of the fuse during battery disconnect.
We discovered that fuselages were SUPPOSED to have been changed to have a longer opening, but that had not actually gotten implemented.
Whiplash from connection during rapid battery exchange removes material
Edge Trim to protect and reduce damage to cut out. Sharp edges can easily cut skin and reduce Flight Op efficiency.

team_view_in_comments: We coordinated to enlarge the cutout for the fuselage to improve access and hopefully reduce the tendency for folks to run their hand into the edge of the fuse during battery disconnect.
reasoning: The description says the cut came from contact with the fuselage edge while removing the HLB. ENG-1344 found the top cutout edge consistently damaged and sharp, with about a quarter inch of clearance, and identified excessive connector demating force as a cause of hand whiplash. The fix (enlarged cutout) was later found not to have been implemented, so the cause is the cutout geometry and edge condition.
notes: No Root Cause field. IMG_0273.MOV (connector demate tool video) is listed only. Safety squawk, no tail number.

event: VXE 510 in fuel cell configuration: during the launch wizard lift rotor check the rear left rotor started then stopped and the system disarmed because the VTOL autopilot had a watchdog reset; ticket became the master tracker for VTOL AP watchdog resets.
component: VTOL AP firmware (FreeRTOS task scheduling / sensor polling), firmware 1.53 release candidate
failure_mode: Software watchdog reset of the VTOL autopilot during lift motor check; candidate mechanisms are blocking in sensor polling and lower priority tasks blocking higher priority tasks.
contributing: Conformal coat intrusion found in J19/J20 interface board connectors (107-107306) on 510, 509 and 511, judged not related to the watchdog
Replacement avionics board APC-1-1375 failed SCO checkout
Customer report of a launch abort was attributed to a bad HLB, not the watchdog

evidence.quote: Preliminary analysis shows a watchdog reset occurred.
Issue in sensor polling (seen in 6 of 6 watchdog cases, unclear if this is symptom or cause)
Lower priority tasks being promoted and blocking higher priority tasks. (Function of FreeRTOS to provide determinism.)
Conformal coat intrusion discovered on 107-107306 Interface board connector.
Hardware inspection revealed conformal coat quality issue, but initial assessments indicate that it is not related
Looks like J20 connector has conformal coat in all of the pins to some degree.

team_root_cause:
In investigation, possibilities identified:
- Issue in sensor polling (seen in 6 of 6 watchdog cases, unclear if this is symptom or cause)
- Lower priority tasks being promoted and blocking higher priority tasks. (Function of FreeRTOS to provide determinism.)
- Other software architectural issues.

would_settle_it.what: VTOL AP event log around the lift rotor check for the watchdog reset reason and which task was blocked
Identified software issues behind the watchdog resets
Embedded software evaluation of VTOL AP findings on the watchdog cause

reasoning: Preliminary analysis of the 510 data showed a VTOL AP watchdog reset caused the rotor to stop and the disarm. Hardware inspection found conformal coat in the interface board connectors, but the team listed that as an excluded cause. The remaining candidates are all in the VTOL AP software (sensor polling seen in all 6 watchdog cases, task priority blocking), so the result is narrowed to the VTOL AP firmware without a single confirmed mechanism.
notes: Consolidated ticket: VXEP-9 and VXEP-161 are duplicates; other watchdog cases (e.g. ENG-2978 on 515 XCOMM) are linked. Rear left rotor (motor 4) was the symptom, not the failed part, so position is left empty. FS2-806 and FS2-603 are not in the export. The customer-reported launch abort is noted in the ticket as caused by a bad HLB.

event: VXE-492 lost link right after climbing to its commanded 700 ft at Camp Lejeune and was never found despite ground and road searches; aircraft loss.
failure_mode: Loss of downlink after launch completion followed by a fly away; aircraft not recovered.
contributing: Main battery voltage dropped by 3 V just before aircraft data stopped
Last data at launch state 16 (LCH_WAITSAFE)
LOS mission was set to execute (InitialLosRtbOverride=0) but the aircraft did not return

evidence.quote: The Aircraft took off and climbed to its commanded altitude of 700ft as soon as it did, the AV lost connection over ETA-2.
Just before the data from the aircraft stops the main battery drops by 3 volts.
The aircraft reaches launch state 16 LCH_WAITSAFE and no more communications transpire. This may be a critical boundary that could be HIL tested.
Closed, no further action possible. Problem ticket moving to Bermuda Triangle.

would_settle_it.what: Aircraft was never found; recovery would allow inspection of main battery, power connectors and avionics
Main battery voltage and current, link quality and event log in the seconds before data stops
Team analysis of the link loss and battery voltage drop

reasoning: The aircraft reached altitude and transition end (launch state 16) and then all communications stopped, and it was never found. The only data clue is a 3 V drop in main battery voltage just before data ended, which could point to a power problem but is not confirmed by any analysis. With no aircraft and no conclusion in the files, the cause is not determined.
notes: Root Cause field is Unknown and the ticket is on the "Bermuda Triangle" list. The converted docx holds only figure captions. RMA-185 and FS2-725 are linked but were not needed for cause.

event: VXE-450 (fuel cell, Trillium HD55) drifted past the LZ after transition to VTOL on RTB at Camp Lejeune and dropped to the ground, burning; duplicate of VXEP-51.
component: lift ESC assembly 107-101631-2 SN 069: soft start MOSFET Q20 and 5V regulator U1
failure_mode: MOSFET Q20 broke down and detached from its solder pad from high heat; the failure destroyed 5V regulator U1, leaving the ESC dead so the front right motor did not respond in VTOL.
contributing: Old date code (about 2018) FDMS86540 MOSFETs with low solderability, suspected borderline solder joint
U1 rated 25 V max with no reverse current diode, so VBATT on U1 cratered it
Front right motor sounded different during launch wizard spin-up
No logic to abort VTOL or revert to fixed wing when a lift motor fails

evidence.quote: Canceling this as it duplicates an incident already created with more info.
Data review found the autopilot commanded correctly, but front right motor did not respond.
Mosfet Q20 found completely detached, R53 nearby also detached, signs of high temperature solder reflow, board damage.
Replacing U1 then allowed normal functionality, despite the still missing MOSFET Q20, R53.

These mosfets are old datecode and their leads have low solderability; if not a ripple current or short problem I suspect a borderline solder joint that melted or broke which lead to overcurrent failure of the mosfet Q20.

reasoning: This ticket was canceled as a duplicate of VXEP-51, which holds the investigation. Flight data showed the front right motor at full throttle with almost no current, and teardown of the surviving front right ESC found Q20 detached with solder reflow and U1 failed; replacing U1 alone restored the ESC. The failed part is therefore the front right lift ESC, with the Q20 breakdown initiating the U1 failure.
notes: Duplicate of VXEP-51; result copied from that investigation. No Root Cause field on this ticket. Initiating cause (old date code MOSFETs, solder joint) is the team suspicion, not proven. Aircraft was a total loss and replaced.

event: VXE 371 at YPG (JHU VBN demo) flew about 1300 to 1500 ft higher than intended after DTED was loaded after launch wizard calibration; operators deleted the DTED, restarted GCS and landed safely (near miss).
component: GCS DTED loading versus launch wizard pitot/altitude calibration
failure_mode: Calibration done with no DTED (ground at 0 ft MSL); DTED then loaded and GCS restarted in flight, so the GCS commanded a climb of the terrain height to hold the same AGL, risking HLB exhaustion in VTOL landing.
contributing: GFE GCS laptop lacked DTED for the YPG area
GCS software does not block launch or force restart when DTED changes (GCSS-99 not implemented)

evidence.file: data/linked/GCSS-99/attachments/16129_RE Issue with loading DTED in flight .msg.md
evidence.quote: The laptop from SGCS1-70 that was used for the Video Based Navigation (VBN) testing at YPG last week did not have DTED loaded for the YPG area.

evidence.file: data/linked/GCSS-99/attachments/16129_RE Issue with loading DTED in flight .msg.md
evidence.quote: I should have cancelled the Launch Wizard, restarted the GCS software, and restarted the Launch Wizard, but in an effort to save time, I elected to do the final Calibration, launch the plane, then restart the software.

evidence.file: data/linked/GCSS-99/attachments/16129_RE Issue with loading DTED in flight .msg.md
evidence.quote: I believe this was due to an uncontrolled GFE laptop that had the GCS software installed by the customer.
When DTED is changed (added/removed), block the starting of the Launch Wizard until GCS Software is restarted.

team_root_cause:
Problem description:
- Launch wizard (at least the pitot calibration) happened without DTED loaded (aircraft thinks it’s at 0ft MSL)
- At some point after calibration, DTED was loaded
- The aircraft flew ~1000 - 1500ft higher than it was supposed to because it didn’t have ground elevation reference during calibration, but after GCS got the DTED (elevation) data it commanded to climb to maintain the same altitude, but above the newly obtained elevation data
- A concern/assumption was made that during the landing aircraft could start the transition to VTOL at a very high altitude and run out of
attachments_read: 16127_Mail - Gabriel Staples - Outlook [altitude too high incident writeup].pdf.md
16129_RE Issue with loading DTED in flight .msg.md
reasoning: The pilot in command wrote that DTED was copied onto a GCS laptop that lacked it, calibration and launch were done before restarting the GCS, and the restart then made the system climb by the terrain height. Engineers agreed with this sequence and called it a software loophole rather than a bug. The cause is the operator sequence, with the GCS not preventing it as a contributor.
notes: Near miss, aircraft landed safely. GCSS-99 (software block) was canceled without work in 2026. The VA-439 pdf conversion drops some letter pairs (ti, tt, ft), so quotes were taken from the .msg conversion.

event: VXE-444 lost fixed wing autopilot power while transitioning from IP2 to IP4 in the landing pattern after a 25 minute test flight, stalled and dove into the ground; near complete loss.
component: FWAP 5V regulator circuit: capacitor C20 on step-down regulator U14
failure_mode: C20 degraded from about 3.3 nF to 0.015 nF, holding U14 off so the FWAP 5V rail collapsed (measured 2.08 V) and the FWAP processor reset or lost power in flight.
contributing: Suspected overcurrent from payload retract (SupIret anomaly), not confirmed
LED D8 on the FWAP broken with charred 5V trace
VTOL controller log also stopped mid-flight

evidence.quote: The 5V rail was measured at 2.08V between J24 Pin 10 and J21 Pin 30 (since Pin 1 was inaccessible on J24 due to the SLS mount).
Faulty C20 was measured out-of-circuit to still be 0.016nF.
I think it was so low it was driving U14 to ground constantly, which kept it from turning on. Thus, no 5V rail.
[03:05:24.624 5733.624] ap link fault during transition/fw flight
Replaced faulty C20, which allowed regulator to supply the 5V rail again. Can now connect to 444 w/out manually powering 5V rail.
I noticed a crazy anomaly on SupIret, which is the analog supervisor for the payload retract current. Looks like it had a short.

team_root_cause: - Capacitor C20 failed which caused the Fixed Wing Autopilot processor to lose power.

would_settle_it.file: VIT2-252_ VXE444 Crash In Landing Pattern, Investigation Details.docx
would_settle_it.what: Source of the overcurrent that may have damaged C20 (payload retract current trace, XCOMM/AP swap results)
Full XCOMM log IRetract and 12V current around CPU time 5730 to 5740 for a current spike

reasoning: XCOMM event log shows an AP link fault in fixed wing flight followed by the FWAP rebooting, and the bench check of the returned avionics box found the FWAP 5V rail at about 2 V while XCOMM supplied 12.8 V normally. C20 measured 0.016 nF instead of 3.3 nF and replacing it alone revived the regulator and the autopilot. The failed part is C20 in the FWAP 5V regulator circuit; whether an upstream overcurrent damaged it was not settled.
notes: Ticket title says XCOM PCB issue, but the investigation found XCOMM normal and the fault on the FWAP. XCL00041.xlsx and VTL00029.xlsx conversions are cut at 150000 characters and cover only pre-flight data; VT230330.txt ends on 2023-03-30 and XC230331 covers earlier sessions, so they were searched for faults and startups rather than read line by line. bevelwcc pdfs have no text.

event: VXE-450 (fuel cell, Trillium HD55) on RTB at Camp Lejeune transitioned to VTOL, drifted past the LZ unresponsive to nudges and dropped to the ground, burning; aircraft loss.
component: lift ESC assembly 107-101631-2 SN 069: soft start MOSFET Q20 and 5V regulator U1
failure_mode: MOSFET Q20 broke down and detached from its solder pad from high heat; the failure destroyed 5V regulator U1, leaving the ESC dead so the front right motor did not respond in VTOL.
contributing: Old date code (about 2018) FDMS86540 MOSFETs with low solderability, suspected borderline solder joint
U1 rated 25 V max with no reverse current diode, so VBATT on U1 cratered it
Front right motor sounded different during launch wizard spin-up
No logic to abort VTOL or revert to fixed wing when a lift motor fails
Motor blade mount bent

evidence.quote: Data review found the autopilot commanded correctly, but front right motor did not respond.
Mosfet Q20 found completely detached, R53 nearby also detached, signs of high temperature solder reflow, board damage.
Replacing U1 then allowed normal functionality, despite the still missing MOSFET Q20, R53.
During the landing sequence there is a time when the right boom is pulling almost no current
In the case that VBATT is applied (as per this incident). The current design is 25V max limited.

These mosfets are old datecode and their leads have low solderability; if not a ripple current or short problem I suspect a borderline solder joint that melted or broke which lead to overcurrent failure of the mosfet Q20.

team_root_cause:
- MOSFET Q20 found detached from solder pad, suggesting breakdown and then solder melting from high heat.
- Failure from the MOSFET then caused the 5V regulator, U1, to be destroyed, which then rendered the ESC inoperable
reasoning: Video and VTOL log data showed the front right motor at maximum throttle with almost no boom current while the others were attenuated, so that motor was not producing thrust. Teardown of the surviving front right ESC found Q20 detached with solder reflow and U1 cratered, and replacing U1 alone restored function. Bench tests in VA-309 reproduced the U1 cratering only with overvoltage under high load, consistent with VBATT reaching U1 after the Q20 failure.
notes: VXEP-44 is the customer-visible duplicate. Initiating cause (old date code MOSFETs and solder joint) is the team suspicion and not proven; design limits of U1 are listed as contributing. "Vehicle 450 incident report[1].pptx" on ENG-3034 failed to convert. Aircraft was a total loss and replaced.
